newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: PM MEETING WITH BACKBENCHERS OVER NATIVE TITLE PLAN
The Prime Minister has begun the task of convincing Coalition backbenchers of the merits of his native title plan.
John Howard is meeting with the Coalition's backbench Aboriginal Affairs committee.
At least two members of the Committee are outspoken critics of the plan, with Queensland Liberal Tony Smith indicating he may cross the floor over the issue.
KENNETT SAYS HANSON DOESN'T OFFER REAL ALTERNATIVES
The Premier, Jeff Kennett, says Independent Federal MP Pauline Hanson is using the strength of Australia's democracy to undermine it.
He says she doesn't offer real alternatives for anything, and her public comments are extremely damaging to the nation.
Mr Kennett says Ms Hanson lacks a proper party organisation, so the candidates her party stands, are likely to have absolutely extreme views.
He says Ms Hanson hasn't taken up his invitation to meet him, and discuss the effect her public statements are having.
PROMINENT CITIZENS GROUP SUPPORTING WIK DECISION
Well-known Australians from a wide range of areas have come together to support the Aboriginal position on Native Title.
The so-called Alliance of Prominent Citizens includes leaders from the arts, the law, the media, sport, academia and church groups.
Around 200 of them have signed a statement calling for a settlement of the Wik dispute which provides justice for Aboriginal people.
The signatories include actor Geoffrey Rush, Q.C. Hal Wootten, author Thea Astley, rugby league veteran Des Hasler and Jewish community leader Mark Leibler.
The statement calls on all political leaders to show courage and integrity to publicly support the High Court's ruling on native title.
CHICKEN PROTESTOR FOILS KENNETT'S SECURITY
In Melbourne, a chicken in a cherry picker managed to breach the security arrangements at the Premier's office this morning.
While the Premier was speaking on Melbourne radio, a loud knocking could be heard in the premier's office.
A union protestor, dressed in a chicken outfit, was perched in a cherry picker outside the premier's office.
The man later called in to speak to the premier, who called him a bloody idiot.
Several hundred protestors marched to Parliament house from a Melbourne radio station after the premier failed to appear for his weekly talk back.
MCDONALD SAYS CONSULTATION CLAIMS "LUDICROUS"
ABC chairman Donald McDonald has described claims there's been a lack of in-house consultation on restructuring at luDicrous.
A letter from the ABC's managerial association claims the board has relied upon external consultants for advice on accomodating a funding shortfall of $55 million dollars.
Speaking on ABC's AM program, Mr McDonald said there had been wide-ranging, even excessive, consultation at all levels within the ABC.
Yesterday the board cut the budget of Radio Australia by more than half, forcing the loss of three language services.
Changes to domestic services will be announced on May the 15th.
NATIONAL INDUSTRIAL CAMPAIGN FORESHADOWED
A senior Newcastle union official has foreshadowed a major national industrial campaign in an attempt to get BHP to reverse its decision to end steelmaking in Newcastle.

Maurie Rudd from the Australian Workers Union says all BHP employees have been called to attend a mass meeting tomorrow morning to discuss support from other unions ahead of a meeting with the ACTU next Monday.
Mr Rudd says BHP is going to get the fight of its life, because unions won't stand by and see Australian jobs exported to asia.
NEW AUSTRALIA-US CRIME TREATY
Law enforcement agencies in Australia and the United States are set to benefit from a new treaty signed in Washington.
Attorney General Daryl Williams says the Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters Treaty will make it easier for crime fighters in both countries.
It's expected to help in the taking of evidence, location and identification of people, execution of search warrants and tracing and confiscation of the proceeds of crime.
Mr Williams says it will also allow the temporary transfer of prisoners between the US and Australia.
